text.p: The cola war spans the globe and in South Africa the slugging match between industry giants Pepsico and Coca Cola is coloured by the politics of the past.
However, as the country has sought to reunite after decades of divisive politics, Pepsi and Coke now find themselves chasing the same market.

Pepsi re-entered South Africa two years ago, after the country's first full democratic elections toppled the former racist apartheid state. The Coke brand, which leased long-term franchises to its bottlers, had remained during white rule.
This situation added a racial element to a business war that in other parts of the world is more based on the usual glossy image-creation.
Pepsi first arrived via a $20 million joint-venture called New Age Beverages sporting high-profile black American investors like actor Danny Glover and basketball star Shaquille O'Neal.
Black townships, such as Soweto near Johannesburg, were early targets for advertising.
"Black empowerment was very important at first," said Japan Pohlwana, marketing director for New Age Beverages.
But Pepsi now puts a strong emphasis on targetting all sections of the South African market. "We want to cross over our marketing, not just blacks. We need to be talking to everybody," Pohlwana said.
Coke is also gunning for the whole market.

The firm recently sealed an advertising deal with South African Olympic gold medal winner Josiah Thugwane in a bid to capitalise on the unique role sport has played in helping South Africans overcome the scars of the past.

"We want to reach every single South African. We chose to link up with him (Thugwane) because he is a real South African hero," said Paul Pendergrass, communications director at Coca-Cola South Africa.

At the moment Pepsi is not yet a national brand, but has established beachheads in the heavily industrialised and populated province of Gauteng, which includes Johannesburg, and the coastal region of KawZulu-Natal, centred on Durban.
But Coke is confident it can contain the threat.
The industry is highly secretive about its sales figures and exact details are jealously guarded by both companies lest they give their rival an edge.

Coke says it is maintaining its dominance. The South African drinks market is worth about 1.6 billion rand ($351 million), with soft drinks making up about 54 percent. Coke says the firm has 76 percent of the soft drinks sector.
"We are confident we can maintain our leadership position at its historical levels," Pendergrass said.
There is no doubt Coke, with 27 plants and six bottling franchises, is bigger than its rival. But Pepsi advances have hit in the areas where the newcomer operates.

Durban-based Coke bottler Suncrush in September posted pre-tax profit for the year to June 30 edging down to 116 million rand from 118 million. An unsually cold winter helped depress sales, but having Pepsi in the area also contributed.
"In a very competitive market, our current margins will be pressurised," chairman Robin Hamilton said in a statement.
Pepsi's overall strategy is to establish operations all over the country. The next stage will be entering the potentially lucrative Cape Town market and Western Cape province.
Pohlwana said Pepsi aimed to be in the Cape some time next year and expected a rapid roll-out from there. "Two years from now we should have national coverage," he said.

Pepsi says the competition is hotting up and has expanded the whole market for both drinks -- a phenonemon that is perhaps never far from the minds of marketing executives engaged on both sides of the "war".
"Competition is very fierce, but it is something that has made the market grow," Pohlwana said.
